manual.p: A module is a sort of "plug-in": a software package that can easily be used by other programmers. Modules can contain methods, classes, constants, and also other modules. We will use the term members for something, such as a method, that a module contains. Some modules are written in Pike, but C and C++ can also be used.
Pike is delivered with a number of useful modules. Here is a list of a few of the more interesting modules.

item.name: Stdio
item.p: This module is used for reading and writing files, and also for communication over the Internet, and for text-based dialogues with the user. We have used the Stdio module in several examples in this tutorial.

item.name: GTK
item.p: A toolkit for creating graphical user interfaces, with windows, buttons and so on.

item.name: Protocols
item.p: Various protocols, i. e. ways of communicating. One of these is Protocols.HTTP, which is used to communicate with World Wide Web servers in order to retrieve web pages. Some other supported protocols are DNS, IMAP, IRC, LDAP, LysKOM, NNTP, SMTP, and TELNET.

item.name: MIME
item.p: Support for coding and encoding using MIME, which is used in electronic mail.

item.name: Calendar
item.p: Support for various calendar and date formats.

item.name: Mysql
item.p: This module lets Pike use SQL database queries, with the mySQL database server.

item.name: Thread
item.p: Support for threaded execution of Pike programs.

item.name: Process
item.p: Functions to start and control other processes.

item.name: Getopt
item.p: Routines to interpret and handle command line options.

item.name: Regexp
item.p: Support for matching so-called regular expressions.

manual.p: Depending on which operating system you are using, and on exactly how Pike was installed on your system, some of these modules may not be available.
